rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
$$l=0,1,2,\dots,(n-1);\qquad m=-l,\dots,0,\dots,+l;\qquad m_{s}=\pm\tfrac{1}{2}$$
$$\text{orbitals in a subshell}=2l+1;\qquad \text{electrons}=2(2l+1)$$
$$\text{orbitals in a shell}=n^{2};\qquad \text{electrons}=2n^{2}$$

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: ❌ n determines shape and l determines size. ✅ n → size/energy (shell); l → shape (subshell).  ·  ❌ l can equal n. ✅ l = 0 to n − 1, so 1s has l = 0 and 2p has l = 1.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: s, p, d, f stand for sharp, principal, diffuse, fundamental — the old spectroscopic series names.  ·  Shell capacities: K 2, L 8, M 18, N 32 (2n²); subshell capacities: s 2, p 6, d 10, f 14.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: **Problem:** Maximum number of electrons with n = 4 and l = 2? **Solution:** 4d subshell: 2(2l + 1) = 2(5) = 10 electrons.  ·  **Problem:** How many electrons in an atom can have n = 3, m = 0? **Solution:** For n = 3: 3s (m = 0 only), 3p (m = 0 available), 3d (m = 0 available) → 1 + 2 + 2 = 6 electrons.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: ❌ mₗ is the spin quantum number. ✅ mₗ gives orientation; spin is mₛ = ±1/2.  ·  ❌ A p subshell holds 3 electrons. ✅ It has 2l + 1 = 3 *orbitals*, so it holds up to 6 electrons.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Solving the Schrödinger equation for the hydrogen atom yields a set of numbers that completely describe the state of an electron. These are the **quantum numbers** — effectively the 'address' of an electron in an atom. Four numbers are needed: principal (n), azimuthal or angular-momentum (l), magnetic (m or mₗ) and spin (s or mₛ).  ·  ### 2. Principal quantum number (n)

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Spin was proposed in 1925 (Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit) after the Stern–Gerlach experiment (1922).  ·  The 4f subshell (l = 3) holds 14 electrons — the width of the lanthanide series.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: The number of orbitals in the M shell (n = 3) is: → C

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Remember the two counting rules: 2l + 1 orbitals per subshell and 2n² electrons per shell.  ·  Check validity sets in the order n ≥ 1, l ≤ n − 1, |m| ≤ l, mₛ = ±1/2 — a favourite one-mark question.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Stern–Gerlach (1922) split a silver atomic beam into two — the first spin evidence.  ·  Degeneracy of the n = 2 level in hydrogen: 4 orbitals (2s + three 2p).

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: **Problem:** Count orbitals with n = 4, l = 3 and the electrons they hold. **Solution:** 2l + 1 = 7 orbitals (4f), holding 14 electrons; nodes: radial 0, angular 3.  ·  **Problem:** Give the designation of an electron with (n, l, m, mₛ) = (4, 2, −1, +½). **Solution:** n = 4, l = 2 → 4d; m = −1 selects one of the five d orbitals; mₛ = +½ — an up-spin electron in a 4d orbital.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: Determines the **shell** (energy level) and, in effect, the size: r ∝ n². Values n = 1, 2, 3, … ∞; the shell letters are K, L, M, N …; maximum capacity of a shell = 2n² electrons (n = 1 → 2, n = 2 → 8, n = 3 → 18, n = 4 → 32). It corresponds to Bohr's orbit number but is now a quantum label, not a path.  ·  ### 3. Azimuthal quantum number (l)  ·  Determines the **subshell** and the *shape* of the orbital. Values l = 0, 1, 2, 3 … (n − 1), i.e. (n − 1) subshells per shell; the letters are s (l = 0), p (1), d (2), f (3). Orbital angular momentum = $\sqrt{l(l+1)}\,\frac{h}{2\pi}$. Within a shell the energies follow the order s < p < d < f, and a subshell holds 2(2l + 1) electrons (s 2, p 6, d 10, f 14).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: $$\mu=\sqrt{u(u+2)}\ \text{BM},\qquad s=\tfrac{1}{2},\ |s|=\sqrt{s(s+1)}\,\hbar=\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\hbar$$  ·  $$l=0,1,\dots,n-1;\quad m=-l,\dots,+l;\quad m_{s}=\pm\tfrac{1}{2};\quad L=\sqrt{l(l+1)}\,h/2\pi$$  ·  ❌ Orbital angular momentum is l(h/2π). ✅ It is √(l(l+1))h/2π.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ mₛ comes from solving the Schrödinger equation. ✅ Only n, l, m do; spin needs the Dirac equation.  ·  ❌ 2n² counts orbitals. ✅ It counts electrons; orbitals in a shell number n².  ·  ❌ All subshells of a shell have equal energy in every atom. ✅ True only for hydrogen; multi-electron atoms order them by penetration.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ Spin means the electron literally spins on its axis. ✅ Spin is an intrinsic quantum property; the classical picture is only an analogy.  ·  ❌ The five d orbitals have five different energies in a free atom. ✅ They are degenerate; ligand or magnetic fields split them.  ·  ❌ A full designation needs only n and l. ✅ A complete state needs all four numbers (n, l, m, mₛ).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ mₛ determines the orbital orientation. ✅ mₗ gives orientation; mₛ gives spin.  ·  ❌ l can take the value n. ✅ l runs 0 to n − 1.  ·  ❌ Two 2p electrons of carbon must have opposite spins. ✅ Hund's rule: parallel spins in different degenerate orbitals first.
